summary: Specifies the use of the Binary Floor Control Protocol over WebSocket, as a new WebSocket subprotocol. WebSocket gives two-way real-time communication between clients and servers, and this makes it a reliable transport for BFCP in new scenarios such as web-based conferencing. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: A web page can keep a phone-line-like connection to a server open. This document lets the meeting "talking stick" rules travel over that connection, so web-based meeting tools can use them too.

questions: how does bfcp work in a web browser
what is the bfcp websocket subprotocol
subtitle: How the Binary Floor Control Protocol rides on a WebSocket connection so browser-based conferencing can use it.

tldr.problem: BFCP, which coordinates access to shared resources in a conference, only had TCP and UDP transports defined, which does not suit web browsers and other WebSocket client stacks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a WebSocket subprotocol named bfcp: each BFCP message travels in one unfragmented binary WebSocket frame, and SDP gets new TCP/WS/BFCP and TCP/WSS/BFCP values plus the websocket-uri attribute.
tldr.outcome: Browser and other WebSocket clients can use BFCP over a reliable transport, with secure WebSocket (WSS) strongly preferred. IANA registered the subprotocol and the two SDP values.

today: RFC 8857 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021. The unit metadata lists nothing that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the BFCP specification in RFC 8855.

sections.title: BFCP Meets WebSocket
sections.content:
The Binary Floor Control Protocol (BFCP, RFC 8855) coordinates access to shared resources in a conference. It is used between floor participants and floor control servers, and between floor chairs (moderators) and floor control servers.

The WebSocket protocol (RFC 6455) gives two-way message exchange between clients and servers over a persistent TCP connection, optionally secured with TLS. Modern web browsers include a WebSocket client stack. RFC 8855 defines two BFCP transports, TCP and UDP. This RFC adds a WebSocket subprotocol, giving BFCP a reliable and boundary-preserving transport. Since WebSocket is reliable, the BFCP extensions for unreliable transports do not apply.
sections.plainLanguage: A conference has a talking stick that decides who may speak or share their screen. This document lets web pages pass the talking stick around too.

sections.title: How WebSocket Works
sections.content:
WebSocket is a transport layer on top of TCP, optionally secured with TLS, where client and server both send message units in both directions. It defines a handshake, subprotocol and extension negotiation, a frame format, a masking mechanism and status codes for disconnections.

The handshake is based on HTTP. The client sends an HTTP GET with an Upgrade header field, and a successful server answers with an HTTP 101 status code, after which the connection upgrades from HTTP to WebSocket. During the handshake the two sides agree on the application protocol to use on top, called a WebSocket subprotocol, which defines the format and meaning of the messages. Unlike plain HTTP, the connection stays open for many exchanges, and because WebSocket has message units it preserves message boundaries.
sections.plainLanguage: The browser knocks using normal web language, the server says yes, and then the line stays open so both can talk whenever they like.

sections.title: The bfcp Subprotocol Handshake
sections.content:
The client and server agree to use the WebSocket BFCP subprotocol during the normal WebSocket handshake. The client MUST include the value bfcp in the Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header field of its request, and the server's 101 reply MUST contain bfcp in the same header field. After that the connection can carry BFCP messages.

A client is a "BFCP WebSocket Client" if it can open outbound connections to WebSocket servers and speak this subprotocol. A "BFCP WebSocket Server" is any BFCP entity that listens for inbound connections from such clients.
sections.plainLanguage: The browser says which language it wants to speak, here called bfcp, and the server has to say it speaks it too before they start.

sections.title: Carrying BFCP Messages in Frames
sections.content:
BFCP messages use a TLV (Type-Length-Value) binary encoding. They MUST therefore be carried in unfragmented binary WebSocket frames (FIN: 1, opcode: %x2). The frame data MUST be a valid BFCP message, so the payload length MUST be lower than the maximum BFCP message size, 2^(16) + 12 bytes. The encoding rules for reliable protocols in RFC 8855 MUST be followed.

Each BFCP message MUST be carried within a single WebSocket message, and a WebSocket message MUST NOT contain more than one BFCP message. The RFC assumes only the binary TLV encoding. A future document might define another, such as JSON serialization, and that would need a new subprotocol identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: One letter goes in one envelope, and every envelope holds exactly one letter. Nothing is split up and nothing is bundled together.

sections.title: Reliability and Who Connects
sections.content:
WebSocket is reliable, so the subprotocol is too. Client and server transactions MUST follow the procedures for reliable transports in RFC 8855 and RFC 8856.

A BFCP WebSocket client cannot receive incoming WebSocket connections from other peers, so it MUST actively initiate the connection to the BFCP WebSocket server. The server has a globally routable address, so ICE is not required, as clients always initiate connections to it.
sections.plainLanguage: The browser always makes the phone call. The server never calls the browser, so the server just needs an address anyone can reach.

sections.title: SDP Values and Attributes
sections.content:
Two new values are defined for the SDP "proto" field: TCP/WS/BFCP for BFCP over WebSocket over TCP, and TCP/WSS/BFCP for BFCP over secure WebSocket, which runs over TLS and TCP. The "m=" line rules come from RFC 8856. Depending on the SDP setup attribute (RFC 4145), the port field is either the port the remote endpoint should send to, or irrelevant and set to 9, the discard port. Secure WebSocket is recommended for security, but TCP/WS is also permitted for maximum client compatibility.

The websocket-uri attribute from RFC 8124 MUST be used when BFCP runs over WS or WSS, and its procedures MUST be followed.

In the offer/answer exchange, both sides MUST create an "m=" line for each BFCP-over-WebSocket stream and give it either value of "proto". The server side, whether offerer or answerer, MUST add a websocket-uri attribute. If a browser sends an offerless INVITE, the server is the offerer, MUST set setup to passive, and MUST include the websocket-uri attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: The call setup note says which kind of line to use, plain or secure, and the server writes down the web address where the browser should connect.

sections.title: Authentication and Security
sections.content:
RFC 8855 says BFCP parties SHOULD authenticate each other and recommends mutual TLS/DTLS. Browser-based WebSocket clients cannot control TLS through the WebSocket API, so standard web-based authentication methods are RECOMMENDED. Clients SHOULD use TCP/WSS. If the signaling used to set up the conference is authenticated and confidentiality and integrity protected, WSS MUST be used and the floor control server MUST authenticate the client. The client follows RFC 7525 for TLS, verifies the server certificate, and the websocket-uri value MUST contain a hostname. The a=fingerprint attribute is not used for this.

A server that receives a message over TCP/WS can demand TCP/WSS by sending a BFCP Error message with error code 9 (Use TLS). To authorize the connection the server SHOULD inspect cookie header fields in the HTTP GET request, or it can ask for HTTP authentication by replying with a 401 status code.

When BFCP runs over WebSocket, the security mechanisms of RFC 8855 are not used. The application relies on the mechanisms in RFC 6455. Because the WebSocket API lets an application choose no encryption algorithm, protection is limited to whatever TLS algorithm the WebSocket library uses.

The RFC walks through the BFCP threats: impersonating a server or a client is avoided by accepting BFCP over WSS only, modification is prevented by WSS, replay is prevented by checking that messages on a WSS connection use an authorized user ID, and eavesdropping is addressed by encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: Use the secure lock whenever you can. The server can refuse an unlocked connection and tell the browser to try again with the lock.

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.content:
The RFC shows a handshake. The client sends a GET with Upgrade: websocket, Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: bfcp and Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13. The server answers HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols with Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: bfcp.

It also shows an SDP exchange. The browser offers m=application 9 TCP/WSS/BFCP * with a=setup:active and a=floorctrl:c-only. The server answers with port 50000, a=setup:passive, a websocket-uri of a wss: address, a=floorctrl:s-only and floor definitions that point at the audio and video streams.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show the exact words the browser and server say to each other to agree on the secure line.
